title: Family Archive Check
user: A household archivist who needs to know that a photo/video collection has complete, readable, independently recoverable copies before handing it to family.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The family-photo archival discussion describes multiple copies, media verification schedules, metadata work, and a future handoff as separate burdens.
An Immich user reports an iOS backup sync still running after seven hours for only 2,066 images, making completion and backup confidence difficult.

recurrence: Two independent 2025-26 threads; the HN thread has a long practical discussion. Severity is high because silent incompleteness is discovered when recovery is needed.
current_workaround: People juggle cloud albums, external drives, checksums, manual spreadsheets, and periodic exports.
incumbents_and_gap: Immich, PhotoPrism, rclone, restic, and digikam cover storage or cataloguing; none gives a nontechnical household a single local pass/fail report for media completeness, readability, duplicate backup coverage, and handoff instructions.
smallest_useful_product: Desktop app that inventories chosen folders and mounted backup targets; checks counts, hashes sampled media, reads EXIF/date coverage, produces a portable recovery manifest and printable handoff sheet. Non-goals: hosting photos, facial recognition, or cloud sync.
success_measure: At least 60% of activated users complete two-target verification and export a recovery manifest within seven days.
monetization: one-time — archive checking is episodic and local, with no service cost.
constraints: Read-only by default; clear warnings before disk scans; preserve filenames and metadata; no cloud upload; test APFS, NTFS, exFAT, and common image/video codecs.
why_distinct: It is a recovery-readiness verifier and family handoff artifact, not another photo manager or backup engine.

title: Sideload Readiness
user: Android power users and small IT teams who need to determine whether a device can safely install, update, and recover approved sideloaded software under changing Android rules.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ask HN explicitly asks how people are preparing for impending Android sideloading changes.
A recovery/ADB sideload update aborts at 99% with a post-install error, illustrating how opaque a failed local update is.

recurrence: A policy-change question plus a concrete recovery failure in the following quarter; severity is high for people dependent on locally installed tools.
current_workaround: Users search forums, run ad-hoc adb commands, discover signing or storage failures after an attempted update, and keep undocumented manual steps.
incumbents_and_gap: ADB, Android Studio, OEM recovery, and F-Droid provide installation paths; they do not provide a device-specific readiness report, rollback checklist, or plain-language failure diagnosis.
smallest_useful_product: Signed desktop CLI with brew/winget/scoop installers that runs read-only adb diagnostics, checks developer options, storage, USB mode, package signer continuity and recovery visibility, then emits a shareable report and recovery checklist. Non-goals: bypassing platform controls, bootloader unlocks, or distributing APKs.
success_measure: In usability tests, 8 of 10 users identify the cause and next safe step for a seeded sideload failure without a web search.
monetization: freemium — a free single-device report supports trust; paid fleet reports are useful to small support teams.
constraints: Must never evade Android security or app-store policy; require explicit USB debugging consent; redact device IDs in exported reports; support Linux, macOS, and Windows.
why_distinct: A diagnostic and recovery planner, rather than an alternative app store or a sideloading circumvention tool.

title: OPDS Shelf Bridge
user: Readers with DRM-free libraries and e-ink devices who want a reliable local shelf that can validate, repair, and move books between Calibre-Web/OPDS and devices.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The request for a clear, open e-reader prompts recommendations spanning Kobo, KOReader, and different renderer/format choices rather than one dependable path.
Foliate cannot retain an OPDS catalog credential even when the user selects Remember Password.

recurrence: Two separate reader-stack requests in March 2025; the pain is persistent because library, catalog, credentials, and device choices are fragmented.
current_workaround: Readers configure Calibre, Calibre-Web, device plugins, OPDS clients, and credentials separately, then troubleshoot failures one protocol at a time.
incumbents_and_gap: Calibre, KOReader, Foliate, and Calibre-Web are capable but are separate products; the missing layer is a local connection test and portable, device-oriented queue.
smallest_useful_product: Cross-platform desktop app that tests OPDS endpoints and credentials, validates EPUB metadata/cover files, builds per-device send queues, and writes a local audit log. Non-goals: ebook sales, DRM removal, or a full reader.
success_measure: 70% of imported catalogs pass a connection-and-download preflight on first run; fewer than 10% of queued transfers require manual file picking.
monetization: one-time — the utility operates only on the user's library and devices.
constraints: Support only user-owned/DRM-free content; store credentials in OS keychain; preserve OPDS authentication privacy; do not scrape stores.
why_distinct: It bridges and verifies the existing open-reader stack instead of cloning Calibre or making a reader UI.

title: VRAM Field Test
user: People buying, reselling, or diagnosing a GPU who need an installable, repeatable memory-integrity test with an understandable report.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker wants a MemTest86+-like VRAM tester; replies point to a repair wiki and an LLM-mediated sequence of CLI tools.
A user cannot test all 96GB on an RTX 6000 PRO because the existing Vulkan tool has a 20GB limit.

recurrence: A direct buyer/diagnostic request and a high-memory hardware limitation within one month. Severity is high: a bad GPU is expensive and failures are intermittent.
current_workaround: Users combine gpu-burn, vendor tools, repair-wiki commands, and stress tests with no standard evidence bundle.
incumbents_and_gap: memtest_vulkan, OCCT, gpu-burn, CUDA samples, and vendor diagnostics exist; they differ by vendor, lack portable reports, and often do not make coverage limitations obvious.
smallest_useful_product: Signed CLI installers that enumerate available VRAM, run safe Vulkan/Metal/DirectX pattern suites, make coverage explicit, capture thermals/clocks, and emit JSON plus a one-page report. Non-goals: overclocking, repair advice, or kernel drivers.
success_measure: On a test matrix, the tool reports usable coverage for at least 90% of detected VRAM and produces a reproducible report on Windows and Linux.
monetization: one-time — resale shops and enthusiasts value a trusted report without ongoing service.
constraints: Stress tests must have thermal/time limits and explicit consent; hardware APIs vary; no claims of certifying all GPU faults; retain no hardware telemetry by default.
why_distinct: The product is a cross-vendor test protocol and evidence report, not another benchmark chart or overclocking panel.

title: Sleep Watt Watch
user: Mac and cross-platform desk users who need to find the app, service, or peripheral that prevents sleep or drains power while a computer appears idle.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ask HN asks whether other Mac users are seeing menu-bar errors, a visible symptom of fragile background utilities.
Deskflow users report high macOS client power use during sleep across a download-installed cross-platform desktop utility.

recurrence: Independent macOS utility failures in 2025-26; severity is medium-high because unattended battery loss and heat are difficult to attribute.
current_workaround: Users inspect Activity Monitor, battery screens, Console, and third-party menu bars manually after the event.
incumbents_and_gap: Activity Monitor, powermetrics, Stats, iStat Menus, and Battery Toolkit expose pieces; they do not capture a before/during/after sleep timeline tied to wake assertions and devices.
smallest_useful_product: Menu-bar desktop utility that records wake/sleep events, power assertions, USB/Bluetooth changes, top energy processes, and a privacy-safe timeline export. Non-goals: force-killing processes, undervolting, or broad device management.
success_measure: In a 20-device pilot, it attributes at least 75% of deliberate sleep-prevention cases to a process or device within one capture cycle.
monetization: one-time — local hardware observability has a clear desktop-utility purchase model.
constraints: Use documented OS APIs and least privilege; transparently state sampling limits; exclude window titles and user content from logs.
why_distinct: It is an event-forensics recorder for idle drain, not a generic system monitor.

title: Freeze Capsule
user: Desktop Linux users who need a useful evidence bundle after a freeze, before they reboot and lose the clues needed to identify a graphics, kernel, or app trigger.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The troubleshooting question elicits SSH, netconsole, dmesg, and journalctl suggestions, with the asker admitting the logs are hard to interpret.
A Cinnamon user says a Chrome popup reliably freezes the whole OS, showing the need to preserve context around a desktop lockup.

recurrence: Two July 2026 reports from different Linux communities; severity is high when a user cannot interact with the machine or retain diagnosis data.
current_workaround: Users reboot, later copy journalctl output, set up SSH/netconsole only after learning the hard way, or post incomplete logs.
incumbents_and_gap: journalctl, apport, coredumpctl, netconsole, and distro bug reporters are powerful but not coordinated for ordinary desktop freezes.
smallest_useful_product: Deb/RPM-installable watchdog that snapshots bounded system/graphics/process context to an encrypted local capsule on watchdog timeout or a user hotkey, then renders a redacted bug-report bundle. Non-goals: remote support, kernel modification, or automated bug filing.
success_measure: At least 80% of induced freeze tests yield a capsule with prior journal, GPU, process, and display-session context after reboot.
monetization: free — a trustworthy local diagnostic tool needs broad adoption and can be supported by optional paid support packs later.
constraints: Strict bounded retention and redaction; clearly disclose that a hard lockup can prevent capture; package as a least-privilege service; respect distro log permissions.
why_distinct: It turns fragmented post-crash commands into an automatically preserved local evidence capsule, not another crash-reporting SaaS.

title: Mail Escape Hatch
user: People leaving or auditing an IMAP provider who need a verified local archive that remains readable, searchable, and attachment-complete outside the mail client.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The search for a good IMAP client brings a workaround chain of mbsync, Maildir, OAuth proxy, NMH, and multiple front ends.
The Thunderbird export extension seeks beta testers for a major rewrite, including overdue PDF export with attachments.

recurrence: Two 2026 discussions reflect the same escape-and-preservation job. Severity is high for legal, personal-history, and provider-exit use cases.
current_workaround: Users sync to Maildir, export client folders, wrestle with OAuth, or rely on a proprietary local profile that is hard to validate.
incumbents_and_gap: Thunderbird, mbsync, offlineimap, MailStore, and ImportExportTools export messages; the unresolved gap is a guided, provider-neutral completeness check with a durable reader bundle.
smallest_useful_product: Desktop app that imports IMAP/Maildir/MBOX, verifies folder/message/attachment counts and hashes, flags OAuth or duplicate anomalies, and writes a portable HTML/EML archive plus manifest. Non-goals: sending email, hosting mail, or replacing a client.
success_measure: 90% of test exports can be reopened without the source client and match server folder/message counts within documented exclusions.
monetization: one-time — mail exit is a high-value, infrequent local task.
constraints: Never transmit mail; use OS keychain for credentials; encrypt local temporary files; preserve legal holds and headers; document provider rate limits.
why_distinct: It is an archive-verification and portable-reader tool, not an IMAP client or cloud mailbox migration service.

title: Offline File Bridge
user: Android users of self-hosted or privacy-first storage who need selected offline folders to be safely usable by other local apps when connectivity is unavailable.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker seeks a way for zero-server apps to synchronize keys and chat history securely across devices, highlighting the practical local-data access problem.
The OpenCloud Android request asks why files marked available offline cannot be accessed outside the app and asks for directory download support; it has 26 reactions.

recurrence: A concrete feature request with 26 reactions plus a separate 2026 local-sync question. Severity is high when users expect offline data but cannot hand it to a viewer/editor.
current_workaround: Users manually export individual files, use a second sync app, or discover an offline boundary only when disconnected.
incumbents_and_gap: Nextcloud, OpenCloud, Syncthing, and Files by Google handle their own storage models; few offer a consent-based, encrypted local bridge for a selected offline directory.
smallest_useful_product: Android APK using the Storage Access Framework to maintain user-approved offline mirrors, show freshness and storage state, and expose a share/open-with action without granting broad filesystem access. Non-goals: replacing the storage service, background cloud crawling, or bypassing scoped storage.
success_measure: In offline-device tests, 95% of files marked ready open through a second target app with an accurate freshness status.
monetization: freemium — a free single-folder bridge establishes trust; paid multi-provider policies suit advanced users.
constraints: Android scoped-storage and battery policies; explicit folder consent; device encryption; no claim that content is current without a successful sync; open-source protocol adapters where licenses allow.
why_distinct: It solves the handoff boundary between an app's offline cache and other local apps, rather than cloning a cloud drive.

title: Android Compat Scout
user: Owners of customized Android phones, vehicle dongles, and niche local apps who need to know why an upgrade or unrooted device no longer supports their setup.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The request for Android with Linux-level customization draws discussion of repurposing phones as mini servers and the growing difficulty of bootloader/configuration work.
A Fermata Auto user reports that a previously workable wireless, no-root setup stopped working after Android 15; the issue has 538 comments.

recurrence: A 538-comment compatibility issue and a separate 2026 customization discussion indicate recurring upgrade breakage. Severity is high for setups assembled from hardware, OS settings, and local apps.
current_workaround: Users downgrade, root, read device-specific threads, toggle settings blindly, or buy another dongle without an evidence trail.
incumbents_and_gap: Android settings, adb, device forums, and vendor companion apps expose fragments; no portable diagnostic summarizes OS build, USB/Wi-Fi roles, permissions, companion versions, and known incompatibility signatures.
smallest_useful_product: Installable desktop CLI that collects a consented adb snapshot, checks declared app/device prerequisites, compares saved before/after snapshots, and creates a private compatibility report. Non-goals: rooting, bypassing Android Auto restrictions, or modifying installed apps.
success_measure: In a 15-device test set, the report differentiates OS/version, permission, connectivity, and missing-component regressions in at least 12 cases.
monetization: one-time — hobbyist and installer support use is periodic and local.
constraints: No security bypasses; require USB-debugging consent; remove serials and account information from exports; avoid advocating unsafe driving interactions.
why_distinct: It is a configuration-diff and diagnosis tool for legitimate local setups, not an Android modification service.

title: Terminal Recall
user: CLI-heavy developers and operators who need to search, preserve, and share a bounded record of terminal/TUI output after it scrolls away or a session exits.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The TUI discussion has users contrasting useful local interfaces with the need to keep command output pipeable and recoverable.
An OpenCode user requests editor-like find for the TUI session buffer; the issue has 51 reactions.

recurrence: A 51-reaction request and an independent terminal-interface discussion show a durable interaction problem, not a single product bug.
current_workaround: People increase scrollback, use tmux logs, copy output manually, or rerun commands and hope the same output appears.
incumbents_and_gap: tmux, screen, shell history, asciinema, and individual TUIs retain pieces; none offers a simple cross-shell local index with intentional redaction and portable excerpts.
smallest_useful_product: CLI installers plus optional TUI that wrap selected commands, retain encrypted local session chunks, provide instant full-text search and redacted export, and expire data by policy. Non-goals: cloud collaboration, keystroke surveillance, or automatic capture of every terminal.
success_measure: Users retrieve a known command/output excerpt from a 10,000-line captured session in under five seconds, with secrets redacted by configured rules.
monetization: freemium — a free local core is credible; teams may pay for policy packs and managed shared redaction rules.
constraints: Opt-in capture only; protect API keys and customer data; support POSIX shells and PowerShell; local encryption and deletion must be verifiable.
why_distinct: It is a privacy-first terminal evidence layer, not an AI coding assistant or a replacement terminal emulator.

title: Legacy App Rescue
user: A person preserving an old Android app or game they legally own who needs to inventory its package, save data, dependencies, and device compatibility without hunting untrusted APK sites.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker seeks a way to recover and run an old mobile game from the 2010s; a reply points them to an untrusted third-party download forum.
A sideload user reports that refresh suddenly fails despite redownloading and re-authenticating, leaving no clear recovery path.

recurrence: Both 2025 reports concern locally controlled mobile software becoming unavailable or unrefreshable. Severity is high for personal creations and legally owned legacy tools.
current_workaround: Users search random APK repositories, use old devices, make screenshots, and repeatedly retry signing/refresh tools.
incumbents_and_gap: adb backup alternatives, APK Analyzer, Titanium Backup, and sideload tools handle narrow pieces; there is no preservation-oriented, provenance-first local record that warns when a package cannot run on a target device.
smallest_useful_product: Desktop CLI that inventories user-supplied APKs and an attached Android device, records hashes/signers/SDK requirements, exports allowed app data where Android permits, and writes a reproducible preservation manifest. Non-goals: APK distribution, DRM removal, cracking, or re-signing third-party copyrighted apps.
success_measure: A user can generate a complete manifest and compatibility verdict for 90% of test APKs without uploading the APK or data.
monetization: one-time — preservation is an infrequent, trust-sensitive local task.
constraints: Respect copyright and platform rules; process only user-supplied files; never host binaries; clearly distinguish metadata recovery from executable compatibility; protect app data.
why_distinct: It preserves evidence and migration options for software a user already has, rather than becoming an APK marketplace.

title: Cloud Exit Drill
user: A privacy-minded household moving data out of major cloud services who needs to practice a local restore and see which folders, media, and app bundles are actually protected.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The family-friendly de-Googled home-lab question says open source can work but will not be hands-off; replies recommend a periodic physical Google Takeout backup.
A Nextcloud macOS client report describes server-side deletion of an app bundle and permanent data loss when a placeholder is refused.

recurrence: A practical 2026 cloud-exit request and a current destructive-sync report show why a backup existing is not proof of recoverability.
current_workaround: Users run Takeout exports, copy drives, and trust sync clients without doing a restore drill or recording exclusions.
incumbents_and_gap: Google Takeout, rclone, Nextcloud, restic, and Time Machine provide exports or backups; none turns a consumer cloud exit into a local restore rehearsal with a human-readable gap report.
smallest_useful_product: Desktop app that ingests exported folder trees and selected backup targets, samples restores into a disposable directory, compares manifests/media readability, flags unsupported app bundles, and produces a repeatable exit-drill checklist. Non-goals: cloud account automation, continuous backup, or data hosting.
success_measure: At least 80% of pilot users finish a documented restore drill and identify one actionable coverage gap or reach a clean pass result.
monetization: one-time — cloud-exit and annual recovery-drill use does not justify a subscription.
constraints: Read-only source handling; never request cloud passwords when an export suffices; clear deletion protections; support large trees incrementally; keep all manifests local.
why_distinct: It verifies a user's exit and recovery posture across existing tools rather than offering yet another sync destination.
